\section{Cost-Aware Routing and Wall-Clock Evaluation} \label{sec:wallclock}

This appendix collects the complete wall-clock study that \Cref{sec:experiments} summarises: the \emph{wall-clock time to a target accuracy} (charged replay time, \Cref{sec:wallclock_protocol}) of the learned router against HINTS, the classical solver alone and the classical methods a practitioner would reach for on these problems (geometric multigrid and preconditioned Krylov methods), for all five classical solvers and three PDEs, on $128^2$, $256^2$ and $512^2$ grids, using the cost-aware instantiation of the greedy rule introduced at the end of \Cref{sec:greedy}. Besides the Poisson and convection--diffusion equations of \Cref{sec:experiments} we add \emph{variable-coefficient diffusion} (\Cref{sec:wc_varcoeff}), on which no Fourier diagonalisation exists and the corrector must be learned from data, and \emph{anisotropic diffusion}, $-\epsilon\,\partial_{x_1}^2 u - \partial_{x_2}^2 u = f$ with $\epsilon = 10^{-2}$ (diffusion tensor $\mathrm{diag}(\epsilon, 1)$), on the same periodic domain with the same forcing distribution. It is the standard model problem on which point-relaxation methods fail to smooth: an error component oscillatory in $x_1$ and smooth in $x_2$ is damped by only $(1-\epsilon)/(1+\epsilon) \approx 0.98$ per Jacobi sweep, and geometric multigrid with point smoothing loses its grid-independent convergence (line relaxation or semi-coarsening would be needed). \Cref{sec:wallclock_protocol} describes the protocol; \Cref{sec:wc_poisson,sec:wc_conv,sec:wc_aniso,sec:wc_varcoeff} collect all results per equation (every grid, every tolerance, every baseline, with significance tests and seed trials); \Cref{sec:wallclock_ens} studies ensembles of one, two and three classical solvers; \Cref{sec:wallclock_overheads} accounts for overheads and training cost; and \Cref{sec:wallclock_assumptions} verifies numerically that the assumptions of \Cref{th:suboptgreedy}, Propositions~\ref{th:weaklyalphasupermodular}--\ref{th:simultaneoussupermodular} and \Cref{th:consistency} hold in these settings.

\subsection{Protocol} \label{sec:wallclock_protocol}

\paragraph{Fast, matched implementations.} A wall-clock comparison is meaningful only if the classical baseline is not handicapped by implementation. All classical operations are therefore implemented as compiled, single-threaded C kernels on the periodic 5-point stencil (\texttt{stencil.c}, built with \texttt{cc -O3}): the residual together with its norm (the stopping test, in one pass), fused (damped) Jacobi sweeps, in-place lexicographic Gauss--Seidel, SOR and symmetric SOR sweeps (forward and backward), a lexicographic line Gauss--Seidel sweep in which every grid line along the strongly coupled axis is solved exactly by a cyclic Thomas algorithm (the line relaxation that anisotropic problems call for), and the full-weighting and bilinear transfers of geometric multigrid, whose V(2,2)-cycles use Gauss--Seidel smoothing---or line Gauss--Seidel smoothing for the anisotropic equation---with rediscretised coarse operators and a direct solve on the $32\times 32$ coarsest grid (measured on one $128^2$ instance, first cycle and asymptotic rate: $0.03$ and $0.08$ on Poisson with point smoothing, $0.005$ and $0.04$ on the anisotropic equation with line smoothing, against $0.25$ and $0.86$ with point smoothing there). At $128^2$ a residual evaluation with its norm costs \caCostRes, a Gauss--Seidel sweep \caCostGs, a V-cycle \caCostMg\ and one corrector call \caCostNo, all measured in the exact per-iteration form in which the benchmark charges them (\Cref{tab:ca_costs_poisson}); an earlier version of this study used numpy/scipy sweeps that were $4$--$5\times$ slower and correspondingly overstated the router's margins (\Cref{sec:wallclock_heldout}). The compiled kernels agree with the numpy/scipy implementations they replace to $2\times10^{-14}$ (relative), the line sweep agrees with a sparse block-triangular solve to $10^{-13}$, and their operators and one-step iterates match the dense reference implementations of the original submission to the reference's own precision (relative error below $10^{-7}$, the reference assembling its matrices in single precision; $10^{-12}$ where the reference is exact); the comparison is an assertion in \texttt{validate\_fast\_pde.py}. In the course of this check we found that the original dense symmetric-GS reference mis-implemented the SSOR scaling (the factor $\omega/(2-\omega)$ was added to $D^{-1}$ instead of multiplying it); it has been corrected, and the wall-clock study uses the standard SSOR throughout. Reference solutions are computed by FFT diagonalization of the same discrete operator, i.e., they are exact solutions of the discrete system, so true errors are available for evaluation at no charged cost; the FFT solve is also reported as a baseline in every table (it is a direct method that exists because these test problems have constant coefficients and periodic boundaries; at $128^2$ the router takes \caFftRatioMin--\caFftRatioMax\ times as long as it, and the variable-coefficient problem of \Cref{sec:wc_varcoeff} has no such solve). All timings are single-threaded CPU measurements (Apple M4 Pro, numpy/scipy/PyTorch, one thread). The benchmark guards against machine drift, which on this machine is caused by macOS background services (media analysis, Spotlight indexing and window-server rendering, which slow the memory-bound corrector call by up to $3\times$ for minutes at a time) and by the scheduler, which moves an idle process to the efficiency cores: before the timed replays of every test instance it re-times a reference operation (one corrector call) and waits for up to $2$\,min, re-checking every $5$\,s and running the reference operation in between (a sleeping process stays on the efficiency cores, where the reference remains slow for the whole wait), while that time is more than $15\%$ slower than the session's reference (the $10$th percentile of the reference measurements taken so far, seeded after $10$\,s of running the reference operation, which is robust to measurement noise and tightens only as genuinely faster states are observed); an instance whose reference is still too slow after the wait, or more than $15\%$ slower than the cell's final reference (the $10$th percentile over all its instances, which catches a session that started in a slow state) or than the median final reference of the other cells of the same equation and grid (which catches a session that was slow throughout), is timed anyway and re-timed at the end of the cell, after waiting up to $5$\,min more (the Poisson and convection--diffusion $128^2$ cells were produced before this in-cell pass existed, and every one of their instances is re-timed with the final driver in a separate pass once the other $128^2$ cells are complete). The guard is a per-instance diagnostic; it does not certify that no drift occurred within a replay. Over the \caDriftN\ instance timings of the study the guard waited \caDriftWaits\ times, \caDriftRetimed\ instances were re-timed, \caDriftFlagged\ remained above the tolerance (largest accepted deviation \caDriftMax\%), and the per-instance ratios and load averages are stored with the results (an earlier confirmatory run had been contaminated by a $3.5$\,h stall of the machine inside one cell, which the harness could not detect). Two accounting checks are reported in \Cref{sec:wallclock_overheads}: the charged time of a router solve is \caChargedFracMin--\caChargedFracMax\% of the outer elapsed time of its replay, and its live time to $h^2$ is \caLiveWuMin--\caLiveWuMax\ times its work-unit time.

\paragraph{Corrector.} The neural corrector is a DeepONet applied to the residual $r = f_h - \mathcal{L}_h^a u^{(t)}_h$ and evaluated on a $64\times 64$ sensor grid, i.e., on the coarser grid obtained by band-limited (FFT) restriction to the modes $|k_1|,|k_2| \le 31$ at every grid size (for the anisotropic equation the sensor grid is $N\times N/4$, i.e., full resolution along $x_1$, so that the band contains every mode the point smoothers cannot damp; the sensor grid is the only PDE-specific hyperparameter of the pipeline; the variable-coefficient equation uses the isotropic $64\times64$ grid); its output is prolongated back to the fine grid by exact trigonometric interpolation, so the correction is band-limited by construction and never injects error into the high-frequency band that the classical smoother owns (\Cref{fig:ca_predictions}). The trunk net is the fixed orthonormal Fourier basis of that band ($p = 3969$ basis functions, as in POD-DeepONet \citep{lu2022comprehensive}), and the branch net is a linear layer on the $4096$ sensor values; it is fit by least squares on $32{,}000$--$64{,}000$ exact (residual, error) pairs of the discrete operator drawn from a mixture of spectral shapes (forcing-like, residual-like, white and randomly tilted spectra), and reaches a validation relative error of $\approx 2\times 10^{-6}$ on every mode of the band. The corrector is applied scale-equivariantly, $C_{\mathrm{NO}}(r) = \|Rr\|\,\mathcal{G}_\theta(Rr/\|Rr\|)$, which preserves $C_{\mathrm{NO}}(0) = 0$ (Proposition~\ref{th:weaklyalphasupermodular}). Its deployed form is therefore a linear, Fourier-structured map---a least-squares approximation of the exact band-limited inverse $P\,(\mathcal{L}_h)_{\text{band}}^{-1}R$ of the discrete operator. Replacing it by that exact inverse changes nothing (development run): on the GS pairing at $128^2$ the cost-aware oracle's median work-unit time to $10^{-8}$ was $4.472$\,ms with either corrector and its decision sequence identical on $13$ of $16$ instances. The gains reported below are thus those of an accurate band-limited spectral correction applied at the right moments; the learned corrector stands in for a spectral inverse that, on these constant-coefficient periodic problems, could also be computed directly. Its cost is dominated by a $4096\times 4096$ matrix--vector product and is therefore almost independent of $N$ (\caCostNo\ at $128^2$, \caCostNoC\ at $512^2$, \Cref{tab:ca_overheads}), i.e., about \caMJacobi\ Jacobi or \caMGs\ GS sweeps at $128^2$ and \caMJacobiC\ Jacobi sweeps at $512^2$ (\Cref{tab:ca_costs_poisson,tab:ca_costs_conv,tab:ca_costs_aniso}). The same corrector is used by HINTS and by all routing policies.

\paragraph{Cost-equalised macro-actions.} Per-iteration costs $c_j$ are measured once per equation and grid on the benchmark machine, for all operations of the study in one interleaved session, in the exact form in which the timed replay charges them---the update given the current residual, then the residual of the new iterate and its norm, i.e. the stopping test---as the median over eleven interleaved blocks of the block median of $100$ repetitions (the minimum and the spread across blocks are stored with the costs); every pairing and ensemble of that grid therefore shares one corrector cost and one calibration. The unit of cost $u$ is one corrector call; every operation is applied $m_j = \max\{1,\mathrm{round}(u/c_j)\}$ times per decision, and these macro-actions are compared by their plain error, i.e. the deployed rule is \Cref{alg:greedy} on macro-actions; only an operation dearer than the unit ($c_j > u$, hence $m_j = 1$) is compared per unit of cost, $(\|e_j\|/\|e^{(t)}\|)^{u/c_j}$, and the surrogate weights $\tilde c_j$ use the same exponent. Which actions are dearer than the unit is read off the cost tables: on the four $128^2$ grids none is, so those cells run exactly \Cref{alg:greedy} on macro-actions (the rule the exhaustive check of \Cref{sec:wallclock_assumptions} verifies); on the larger grids only a multigrid cycle can be dearer than the unit (\textbf{[pending]}), and in the granularity ablation of \Cref{sec:wallclock_granularity} the corrector itself is. \Cref{tab:ca_costs_poisson,tab:ca_costs_conv,tab:ca_costs_aniso} list $c_j$, $u$ and $m_j$ for every cell; the equalisation is exact up to rounding ($m_j c_j/u$ lies within $1/(2m_j - 1)$ of $1$). Ensembles reuse the cached pairwise costs of their members, so every member has the same macro-action size in the ensemble as in its pairwise run. The cost-aware oracle runs \Cref{alg:greedy} on these macro-actions with the true error; the \emph{greedy oracle} rows run the cost-agnostic \Cref{alg:greedy} on single operations, as in the main text. (An earlier version of this study applied the exponent $u/(m_j c_j)$ to every action, including the rounding error of cheap ones, which is not \Cref{alg:greedy}; the deployed rule was changed so that the theory covers it.)

\paragraph{Lightweight router.} The learned router selects macro-actions from $6 + K$ scalar features, all $O(1)$ given the residual norm that any stopping test computes: the log relative residual, its per-iteration change over the last macro-action and an exponential moving average thereof, the log epoch index, a one-hot encoding of the previous macro-action, and the log counts of corrector calls so far and of iterations since the last call. It is a two-hidden-layer MLP (64 units) evaluated in numpy, costing $\approx 5\,\mu$s per decision in a warm loop and \caDecInSituMin--\caDecInSituMax\,$\mu$s in situ, where every decision after a macro-action finds cold caches (measured inside the timed replays, \Cref{sec:wallclock_overheads}), independently of $N$. It is trained with the surrogate of \Cref{section:surrogate}, with the per-state weights $\tilde c_k$ normalised by $\sum_k \tilde c_k$ (which does not change the Bayes decision), on states visited by oracle rollouts with $\varepsilon$-exploration (probability $0.1$), followed by two to three DAgger rounds \citep{ross2011reduction} in which the current router's own rollouts are relabelled by the oracle---the batch analogue of the scheduled sampling used in \Cref{sec:training details}. Training uses $32$--$128$ instances per round (fewer on the larger grids) drawn from the same GRF distribution as the test set but with a different seed; the router of every pairing is trained in seconds to a few minutes. Ensemble routers, which must additionally learn to choose among classical members, use a larger imitation budget ($256$ rollouts at $128^2$ and $128$ at $256^2$, six DAgger rounds, hidden width $128$, $300$ epochs): with the pairwise recipe the router over $\{\text{Jacobi}, \text{Jacobi (0.67)}\}$ imitated its oracle imperfectly at tight tolerances (convection--diffusion, $128^2$, $\varepsilon = 10^{-8}$: $3.34$ against the oracle's $2.67$ work-unit ms), which the larger budget removes ($2.70$). At $512^2$ the routers are trained from $32$ oracle rollouts of at most $400$ iterations (stopping error $10^{-8}$); for the convection--diffusion Jacobi pairing, where the first such router missed $h^2$ within the cap on $4$ of $16$ instances, the reported router uses $64$ rollouts of at most $800$ iterations---the only per-cell change to the recipe.

\paragraph{Baselines and metric.} HINTS applies the corrector every $\tau$-th iteration, first at iteration $\tau$ (\Cref{sec:hybridframework}). \citet{zhang2024blending} use the proportion $1/15$ (one DeepONet call per $14$ relaxation sweeps) in all of their two- and three-dimensional experiments and $1/25$ only in the one-dimensional Poisson experiment; since all our problems are two-dimensional, the reference schedule is $\tau = 15$, and $\tau = 25$ is reported as well (an earlier version of this study used it as the reference; the corresponding margins are \caSpHintsTFMin--\caSpHintsTFMax\ at $h^2$ and \caSpHintsTFDeepMin--\caSpHintsTFDeepMax\ at $10^{-8}$ on the $128^2$ pairwise cells). We further report the \emph{best fixed schedule}, selected \emph{per cell and per tolerance} on the test instances themselves (an optimistic baseline), from the family of HINTS with $\tau \in \{2, 5, 10, 15, 25, 50\}$, phase-shifted HINTS with the first call at iteration $0$ and $\tau \in \{5, 10, 15, 25, 50\}$, and the \emph{one-shot schedule}---the corrector once at iteration $0$, then the classical solver only---which is the static rule closest to what the router learns at truncation level and therefore the natural ablation for state-dependent routing ($\tau = 1$, the corrector at every iteration, never reduces the error outside the corrector's band and is omitted); and the best of three \emph{residual-decay rules}, deterministic controls that decide at the router's granularity from the same residual norm that the stopping test computes: the corrector at iteration $0$, then the solver's macro-action, and the corrector again whenever the per-iteration contraction of the residual over the last macro-action was worse than $\theta \in \{0.9, 0.95, 0.98\}$ (the threshold is selected per cell and tolerance on the test set, like the best fixed schedule); like the router, the rule is executed live in the timed replay, its decision statistic and threshold test are charged, and its decisions are verified against the untimed trace. The classical methods without corrector run on the same stencil, with the same accounting, \emph{inside the same replay loop as the policies}---same instance, same warm-up, same random order, same three replays: multigrid V(2,2) alone; conjugate gradients, CG preconditioned by symmetric GS and by a symmetric V-cycle (forward and backward GS, both compiled) for Poisson; BiCGSTAB, multigrid-preconditioned BiCGSTAB and restarted GMRES(20) for convection--diffusion (GMRES is accounted at the granularity of its restart cycles and is not run at $512^2$); point-smoothed and line-smoothed multigrid, CG and its two preconditioned variants for anisotropic diffusion; and the sparse direct solve with a cached factorisation together with the multigrid and CG variants for variable-coefficient diffusion. The Krylov methods are SciPy implementations driven by the compiled matrix--vector product and preconditioners: their per-iteration true errors come from an untimed pass with a callback, and the timed pass runs exactly the same number of iterations with a timestamp-only callback (a few hundred nanoseconds per iteration) and verifies that it made exactly that many iterations and that its final iterate reaches the error the untimed pass recorded to within $10\%$ (largest ratio of the two final errors over the study: \caKrylovCheckMax; runs failing either check are excluded from the comparisons and counted: \caKrylovInvalid). An earlier version of this study timed the classical baselines in separate sessions; the same computation differed by $4$--$9\%$ between sessions on identical instances (paired, $p < 10^{-4}$), so every cross-session $p$-value was uninformative, which is why all baselines are now timed in-session. All configuration choices of the study were made on a development test set (GRF seed $72$, with the earlier numpy kernels, the earlier forcing sampler and $\tau = 25$ as reference; archived as \texttt{results\_dev/}); the results reported here are a single confirmatory evaluation of the frozen configurations on a fresh test set (seed $73$) with three timed replays per instance, and \Cref{sec:wallclock_heldout} places the two side by side. The test forcings are drawn from the hierarchical GRF of \Cref{sec:experiments} as real white noise filtered in Fourier space, which realises exactly the stated covariance with the Hermitian symmetry of a real field (the development runs used a sampler that drew independent complex coefficients on the half-spectrum, which halved the variance of the modes on the $k_2 = 0$ line); the Nyquist modes are excluded, so every forcing is a trigonometric polynomial with $|k| < N/2$ in both directions, and the instances are drawn sequentially so that the first $n$ instances of any script are the benchmark's. For each test instance ($64$ at $128^2$; $32$ at $256^2$, except $16$ for anisotropic diffusion; $16$ at $512^2$) we record, after every iteration, the true relative error $\|e^{(t)}_h\|/\|u_h\|$ (untimed, benchmark-only) and the cumulative charged wall-clock time of a replay that executes only the chosen operations (residual and its norm, update, and---for the learned router---every feature and decision computation; oracle decisions are not charged). The reported time to a tolerance is the charged time at the first iteration whose true error is below it, identically for every method: it is a benchmark of the work needed to reach an error level, not of a deployed stopping rule (which would stop on the residual norm that every method computes anyway). We report the median first time at which the error drops below a tolerance $\varepsilon$; paired speedups---the median over instances of the per-instance time ratio, which is the estimand behind every speedup and test in the speed tables and in \Cref{tab:ca_main} (the time tables show medians of raw times for scale, which can order differently from the paired median on small samples, and their bold marks compare those raw medians within a pairing)---with bootstrap $95\%$ intervals ($2000$ resamples over instances) and two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on the paired log time ratios (the direction is read from the median ratio; ``slower'' marks a median below one); the study performs several hundred such tests, so the speedup tables mark as significant only comparisons that survive a Holm correction at level $0.05$ over all tests of the table. A run that does not reach $\varepsilon$ within the iteration cap ($60{,}000$ at $128^2$, $40{,}000$ at $256^2$, $8{,}000$ at $512^2$; $5{,}000$ units for the classical baselines, $3{,}000$ at $512^2$) is marked $\dagger$ with the number of censored instances; a median time over runs of which any is censored is the median of the mixed vector of reached times and times-to-cap, a lower bound, and is marked $\geq$ (invalid runs are dropped and counted with $\times$). In the paired comparisons the four censoring classes are decided from the censoring indicators before any substitution: a censored baseline run enters at its time-to-cap (marked $\S$ with its count), so that the median ratio is a lower bound on the true ratio whenever such caps are present and neither of the two following classes occurs (then marked $\geq$); a censored router run enters as a ratio of $0$ and as the most extreme negative rank in the test, i.e. a failure penalty counted against the router (marked $\dagger$ with its count); a pair in which both are censored carries no information about the true ratio and is excluded from the median and the test (marked $\ddagger$ with its count); and a pair with an invalid run is dropped (marked $\times$). The estimand is therefore the paired median of capped-time ratios with a failure penalty for the router, not a ratio of ordinary completion times, and the $p$-values and intervals refer to that convention; a cell with fewer than four informative pairs prints no ratio. Every affected cell carries its class counts. Timed replays are repeated three times per instance in a random order over policies and baselines, each replay preceded by an untimed warm-up (one corrector call and one sweep, or the baseline's own operation) so that every method starts from the same cache state---the corrector's matrix exceeds the CPU caches, and without the warm-up a policy's first call was up to $0.1$\,ms slower or faster depending on which policy had run before it; the median over replays is used. The measured per-operation costs set the macro-action sizes and define \emph{work units} (measured per-iteration costs times executed operations, plus the measured decision cost per decision), a timer-free measure of the decision sequence used wherever runs from different sessions must be compared; all reported live times are measured directly. We highlight $\varepsilon = h^2$ as a nominal grid-dependent tolerance and checked on the confirmatory instances themselves (\caDiscN\ instances over all equations and grids) whether it lies below their discretisation error: comparing the exact discrete solution with the exact discrete solution on a four times finer grid for the same forcing (\texttt{discretization\_error.py}; for variable coefficients the coefficient is one grid-independent function), the relative discretisation error, estimated as the difference between the two discrete solutions, has median \caDiscMedMin--\caDiscMedMax\,$h^2$ over the equations and grids, and its smallest ratio to $h^2$ over all instances is \caDiscMinHsq; wherever that ratio exceeds one, $h^2$ is a tolerance below the (estimated) discretisation error, and driving the algebraic error further is unlikely to improve the computed solution materially (the two error components can partly cancel, so ``never'' would be too strong); we also report $10^{-3}$ and $10^{-8}$, and the iteration-based metrics of the main text (AUC $=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|e^{(t)}_h\|/\|u_h\|$ over $T = \caT$ iterations, compared by paired $t$-tests on $\log\mathrm{AUC}$) on the $128^2$ grid. Every router was additionally retrained from scratch with five independent seeds (different training instances, exploration and initialisation; the corrector and the test set are fixed) and re-run on the test set; because those trials ran in separate sessions, whose live timings are not comparable with the main run's, they are compared in work units.

\subsection{Poisson} \label{sec:wc_poisson}

\Cref{tab:ca_time_poisson} collects the median time to $10^{-3}$, $h^2$ and $10^{-8}$ for every pairing, every policy and the classical baselines on all three grids; \Cref{tab:ca_speed_poisson} the paired speedups of the learned router with their $p$-values; \Cref{fig:ca_usage_poisson,tab:ca_usage_poisson} where the iterations go; \Cref{tab:ca_costs_poisson} the measured costs and macro-action sizes; \Cref{tab:ca_auc_poisson} the iteration-based metrics; and \Cref{tab:ca_seeds_poisson} the seed trials.

\paragraph{Two regimes.} At $\varepsilon = h^2$ the router makes one corrector call on \caOneCallMin--\caOneCallMax\% of the instances (over all $128^2$ pairwise cells) and then smooths (\Cref{tab:ca_usage_poisson}): the router executes the same decision sequence to $h^2$ as the best static schedule on \caAgreeBestMin--\caAgreeBestMax\% of the instances and as the cost-aware oracle on \caAgreeOracleMin--\caAgreeOracleMax\% (over all $128^2$ pairwise cells, every equation; \Cref{sec:experiments}) and the router's paired ratio against the best fixed schedule is close to one (\Cref{tab:ca_speed_poisson}; bold marks the comparisons that remain significant after the Holm correction), while HINTS with its published period, whose first call comes after $\tau - 1$ wasted sweeps, is slower by the factors in the table; the ratio of the solver alone to the router ranges over \caSpSolverMin--\caSpSolverMax\ over all $128^2$ pairwise cells (every equation), the low end being the \caSpSolverMinPairing\ pairing (multigrid alone reaches $h^2$ in a few cycles: \caVsMgEnsAllMin--\caVsMgEnsAllMax\ against the $\{\mathrm{NO}, \text{multigrid}\}$ router). Below $h^2$ the remaining error is the band the corrector cannot see, and the schedules separate: the router calls the corrector again only when the smooth error has re-emerged (two or three calls down to $10^{-8}$; \Cref{fig:ca_usage_poisson}), the one-shot schedule never calls it again and pays for hundreds of extra sweeps, and a periodic schedule keeps paying for calls whether or not they help, so at $10^{-8}$ the paired ratios against HINTS and the one-shot schedule are \caSpHintsDeepMin--\caSpHintsDeepMax\ and \caSpOneshotDeepMin--\caSpOneshotDeepMax\ over all $128^2$ pairwise cells (every equation), whereas against the best fixed schedule and the best residual-decay rule---both selected on the test set---the outcome depends on the pairing (\Cref{tab:ca_speed_poisson}; the counts over all pairings are in \Cref{sec:experiments}, and \Cref{sec:wallclock_granularity} tests whether the macro-action granularity explains the losses). The cost-agnostic greedy oracle (\Cref{alg:greedy} on single operations) makes the same decisions as its cost-aware counterpart on the path to $h^2$ (they differ later, in when the corrector is called again); the ratio of the learned router's median time to the cost-aware oracle's is \caSpOracleRatioMin--\caSpOracleRatioMax\ and the two execute the same decision sequence to $h^2$ on \caAgreeOracleMin--\caAgreeOracleMax\% of the instances (over all $128^2$ pairwise cells), and the five retrained routers are compared with the main router in \Cref{tab:ca_seeds_poisson} \textbf{[pending]}.

\paragraph{Classical baselines and larger grids.} Against the classical methods without corrector (bottom block of \Cref{tab:ca_time_poisson}; timed in the same session as the router of every pairing), multigrid alone has the smallest ratio to the router among the classical methods in the current cells: at $128^2$ the paired ratio of multigrid alone to the router (above one favours the router; over all $128^2$ pairwise cells) is \caVsMgAllMin--\caVsMgAllMax\ at $\varepsilon = h^2$ and \caVsMgDeepMin--\caVsMgDeepMax\ at $10^{-8}$, because one corrector call removes the modes $|k|\le 31$ at the price of one matrix--vector product whereas a V(2,2)-cycle contracts the whole spectrum by $\approx 0.03$ on the first cycle and $\approx 0.08$ asymptotically; routing over $\{\mathrm{NO}, \text{multigrid}\}$ calls the corrector once and lets the cycles remove the rest (\caVsMgEnsAllMin--\caVsMgEnsAllMax\ of multigrid alone at $h^2$ and \caVsMgEnsDeepMin--\caVsMgEnsDeepMax\ at $10^{-8}$), and the ratio of multigrid-preconditioned CG to the router is \caVsKrylovAllMin--\caVsKrylovAllMax\ at $h^2$ and \caVsKrylovDeepMin--\caVsKrylovDeepMax\ at $10^{-8}$. The FFT direct solve, exact for this constant-coefficient periodic problem, is the reference the router takes \caFftRatioMin--\caFftRatioMax\ times as long as at $128^2$ and $1.5$--$2.3$ times as long as at $256^2$ (\Cref{tab:ca_speed_poisson}). At $256^2$ the macro-actions are shorter ($15$ Jacobi, $4$ Gauss--Seidel, $2$ SymGS sweeps per corrector call, \Cref{tab:ca_costs_poisson}), so every schedule period that beat the router at $128^2$ fits inside one macro-action, and the picture below truncation level changes: at $10^{-8}$ the router is significantly faster than the best fixed schedule of the test-set search in the Jacobi ($1.28\times$, $31$ of $32$ instances), SOR ($1.12\times$) and damped-Jacobi ($1.06\times$) pairings and within $2\%$ of it in the Gauss--Seidel, SymGS and multigrid pairings, with the cost-aware oracle at $1.00$--$1.30\times$; at $h^2$ it stays within $1$--$3\%$ of the best schedule and is $1.4$--$4.1\times$ faster than HINTS ($\tau{=}15$) and $1.6$--$2.8\times$ faster than multigrid alone in every pairing (\Cref{tab:ca_speed_poisson}). At $512^2$ \textbf{[pending]} the corrector's fixed band $|k|\le 31$ leaves the smoother all modes $k \ge 32$, whose slowest member contracts by only $0.98$ per Jacobi sweep (against $0.71$ at $N=128$): every schedule then needs the same $\approx 80$ sweeps after the first call, the wall-clock time is dominated by sweeps, and the corrector---whose cost is nearly grid-independent---is worth fewer of them, so the best classical method at $512^2$ is expected to be multigrid, alone or with one corrector call, the limit of a corrector whose band does not grow with the grid.

\subsection{Anisotropic diffusion} \label{sec:wc_aniso}

The anisotropic equation is where the two components of the hybrid are most complementary and where the point smoothers are weakest: they damp the $x_1$-oscillatory modes only by $(1-\epsilon)/(1+\epsilon) \approx 0.98$ per sweep (none of the five point smoothers alone reaches $h^2$ within the iteration cap at $128^2$, \Cref{tab:ca_time_aniso}), whereas the corrector, whose sensor grid keeps full resolution along $x_1$, removes exactly those modes together with the smooth ones in a single call and leaves the smoother only the $x_2$-oscillatory band, which it damps at the isotropic rate. The corrector's $N \times N/4$ band is thus the spectral counterpart of semi-coarsening, and the honest classical comparison is the method a practitioner would use on this problem: \emph{line} Gauss--Seidel along $x_2$ (which contracts the $x_1$-oscillatory modes by $0.35$--$0.45$ per sweep, measured on the modes $(N/2, 0)$ and $(N/4, 0)$ at $128^2$, where point Jacobi contracts them by $0.98$) and line-smoothed multigrid, which regains grid-independent convergence (asymptotically $\approx 0.04$ per cycle on one $128^2$ instance, against $\approx 0.86$ with point smoothing). Both are included, line GS as the sixth pairing $\{\mathrm{NO}, \text{line GS}\}$ and, together with point-smoothed multigrid and the CG variants, as classical baselines timed in the same session; against point-smoothed multigrid and multigrid-preconditioned CG the router is faster in every pairing at both tolerances except the Jacobi pairing at $10^{-8}$ (\Cref{tab:ca_speed_aniso}). For the point-smoother pairings the router reaches $h^2$ in the time of one corrector call plus a few sweeps, as does the one-shot schedule, while HINTS ($\tau{=}15$) is $1.4$--$2.8\times$ slower there and the best fixed schedule, one call at $t=0$ followed by sweeps, is $4$--$5\%$ faster than the router, the cost of the router's per-step decision (\Cref{tab:ca_speed_aniso}). At $10^{-8}$ the router is faster than the best fixed schedule in the Jacobi pairing ($1.7\times$), at parity in the GS, SymGS and damped-Jacobi pairings, and slower in the SOR ($0.95\times$) and line-GS ($0.83\times$) pairings, the latter being one whose best schedule has a period shorter than a macro-action; the five-seed trials for this equation are \textbf{[pending]} (\Cref{tab:ca_seeds_aniso}). The $512^2$ grid is not run: the anisotropic corrector keeps full resolution along $x_1$ ($N\times N/4$ sensors), so at $512^2$ its least-squares branch would be a dense $65{,}536\times 65{,}536$ matrix ($17$\,GB in single precision), which the current design cannot hold; a coarser $x_1$ resolution would leave the point smoothers modes they cannot damp (\Cref{sec:wallclock_ens} discusses exactly this regime).

\subsection{Variable-coefficient diffusion} \label{sec:wc_varcoeff}

The three equations above have constant coefficients on a periodic domain, so their discrete operators are diagonalised by the FFT: the exact band-limited inverse that the corrector approximates has a closed form, and a direct FFT solve is available, which at $128^2$ takes $1/$\caFftRatioMax--$1/$\caFftRatioMin\ of the best router's time (\Cref{tab:ca_time_poisson,tab:ca_time_conv}). To evaluate the hybrid where neither exists we add $-\nabla\cdot(a(\mathbf{x})\nabla u) = f$ on the same periodic domain with a fixed, smooth, positive coefficient field $a(\mathbf{x}) = \exp(\kappa z(\mathbf{x}))$, where $z$ is a band-limited random field ($|k| \le 4$, one fixed realisation, scaled by its maximum on a fixed $1024^2$ reference grid, so that $a$ is one grid-independent function sampled on every grid) and $\kappa = \tfrac12\ln 10$, so that the contrast $\max a / \min a$ is at most $10$ by construction ($9.99$ measured on the grids used); the forcing distribution is unchanged. The discretisation is the conservative 5-point scheme with face-averaged coefficients (symmetric positive semidefinite, constants in its null space); reference solutions come from a sparse LU factorisation with one pinned unknown, which is also reported as a direct-solve baseline (its solve time with the factorisation cached, the factorisation itself costing $\approx 0.5$\,s at $128^2$). Geometric multigrid rediscretises the coarse operators with block-averaged coefficients and contracts the error by $\approx 0.1$ per V(2,2)-cycle. The corrector is the same least-squares DeepONet as before---a linear map on the $64\times64$ band---but fitted to (residual, error) pairs of \emph{this} operator, whose band-limited inverse $R\,(\mathcal{L}_h)^{-1}P$ is not diagonal in the Fourier basis and has no closed form. It is nevertheless a fixed $4096 \times 3969$ matrix that could be assembled directly from $4096$ sparse solves, one per sensor basis function; the least-squares fit on random pairs recovers it to the same $\approx 10^{-6}$ as on the constant-coefficient equations. What changes is that this matrix is no longer the inverse of the band-restricted error: a variable coefficient couples the band to the modes outside it, so an out-of-band residual leaves band error that the corrector does not see, and a band correction leaves out-of-band error behind. That coupling, not fit error, is why the corrector is called repeatedly along a solve and why the router's decisions matter beyond the first call; what this experiment tests is routing on an operator without Fourier structure (no shared eigenbasis with the smoothers), not that the correction must be learned. The coefficient field is fixed rather than sampled, so this experiment tests a corrector learned for one operator without an analytic inverse, not generalisation across coefficient fields; the latter would require the coefficient-conditioned branch of the original DeepONet and is left to future work. \Cref{tab:ca_time_var,tab:ca_speed_var,fig:ca_usage_var,tab:ca_usage_var,tab:ca_costs_var,tab:ca_auc_var,tab:ca_seeds_var} report the same quantities as for the other equations on the $128^2$ and $256^2$ grids.

\subsection{Decision granularity} \label{sec:wallclock_granularity}

The cost-aware router decides once per macro-action, and the macro-action of a cheap solver is as expensive as one corrector call---\caMJacobi\ Jacobi or \caMGs\ Gauss--Seidel sweeps at $128^2$ with the compiled kernels. Below truncation level the best fixed schedules at $10^{-8}$ are \caBestDeepSchedList\ (pairings in parentheses), the periodic ones among which call the corrector more often than a cost-equalised macro-action of \caMGs\ Gauss--Seidel or \caMJacobi\ Jacobi sweeps allows the router to, a plausible cause of the router's losses in several pairings at $10^{-8}$ (\Cref{tab:ca_speed_poisson,tab:ca_speed_conv,tab:ca_speed_aniso}). The granularity is a free parameter of the construction of \Cref{sec:greedy}: the unit of cost can be any fraction of a corrector call, actions dearer than the unit (here the corrector itself) being compared per unit of cost. \Cref{tab:ca_granularity} repeats the $128^2$ study with the unit set to one quarter of a corrector call (about a quarter of those sweeps per decision; the corrector is then the one action dearer than the unit and is scored per unit of cost), routers retrained with the same recipe, on the same confirmatory instances, for every pairing and for the nested two-member Jacobi ensemble.

\begin{table}[H]
\color{red}
\centering

\subsection{Solver ensembles} \label{sec:wallclock_ens}

\paragraph{When can a second classical solver help?} The cost-aware oracle is a per-decision comparison of macro-actions, so a router over $\mathrm{NO}\cup\mathcal{W}$ can only beat the best pairwise router of its members if, along the way to the tolerance, the error passes through regimes in which \emph{different} members give the largest reduction per unit cost. We screened this ceiling exhaustively before training any router: for every subset $\mathcal{W}$ of up to three members of $\{$Jacobi, Jacobi (0.67), GS, SymGS, SOR (1.5), multigrid$\}$ (multigrid on the isotropic equations only), every equation and grid, we ran the cost-aware oracle over $\mathrm{NO}\cup\mathcal{W}$ on the test instances and compared its work-unit time to that of the oracle over each member alone (\Cref{tab:ca_ens_screen}). Two facts emerged in the development screening (\textbf{[provisional]}). At $\varepsilon = h^2$ no ensemble beat the best single solver anywhere: one corrector call followed by one or two macro-actions of the cheapest smoother already reaches truncation-level accuracy, so there is no second regime to exploit. At $\varepsilon = 10^{-8}$, after the corrector has removed the smooth band, the smoother has to damp the whole band $|k| > 31$, whose sub-bands favour different solvers: undamped Jacobi is the cheapest per unit cost on the modes near the band edge (it contracts them by $\cos(2\pi\cdot 32/N)$-like factors that damped Jacobi cannot match), but it does not damp the near-Nyquist modes at all, which damped Jacobi and GS remove in a few sweeps. In the development screening (\textbf{[provisional]}: \Cref{tab:ca_ens_screen} is computed with the development-run macro-action sizes; the confirmatory screening with the compiled kernels' sizes is pending) the oracle over $\{\text{Jacobi}, \text{Jacobi (0.67)}\}$---a \emph{nonstationary} Jacobi iteration whose damping parameter is chosen per macro-action---was therefore faster than every single solver, by $13$--$28\%$ on four of the six (equation, grid) settings at $128^2$ and $256^2$, and adding a third member (GS) changed nothing, i.e., the gain saturates. Whether this ceiling survives the coarser macro-actions of the compiled kernels is exactly what the nested-ensemble runs below measure. At $512^2$ (development screening) multigrid dominated every subset (its cycle removes all sub-bands at once), so the oracle over any ensemble containing it equalled the oracle over $\{\mathrm{NO}, \text{multigrid}\}$: adding members neither helped nor hurt. The ``difficulty'' that matters for ensembles is thus not the equation but the width of the spectrum left to the classical members after the corrector, which grows with the grid (fixed band) and with the tolerance.

\paragraph{Nested ensembles.} \Cref{tab:ca_ens_nest} evaluates the learned router over the nested sets $\{\text{Jacobi}\}$, $\{\text{Jacobi (0.67)}\}$, $\{\text{Jacobi}, \text{Jacobi (0.67)}\}$ and $\{\text{Jacobi}, \text{Jacobi (0.67)}, \text{GS}\}$ on every equation at $128^2$ and $256^2$, and at $128^2$ also over the four ensembles of \Cref{sec:experiments} ($\{\text{Jacobi}, \text{GS}\}$ up to all five solvers); the single-member routers are the pairwise routers of \Cref{sec:wc_poisson,sec:wc_conv,sec:wc_aniso}, evaluated in the same session on the same instances, and all members keep the macro-action sizes of their pairwise runs. The table reports live and work-unit times to $h^2$, $10^{-6}$ and $10^{-8}$ for the router and its oracle, and the paired speedup at $10^{-8}$ over the best single-member router (and of the ensemble oracle over the best single-member oracle) with its $p$-value; work units are the primary measure, since they are determined by the decision sequence alone. The $128^2$ cells and the Poisson $256^2$ cells are final under the revised protocol; the other $256^2$ cells are \textbf{[pending]}. \emph{Separation}: at $\varepsilon = 10^{-8}$ the ensemble router is faster than every single-member router by at least $10\%$ and significantly so (bold in the table) in \caNestWins\ of the \caNestNum\ ensemble cells, and the ensemble \emph{oracle} is \caNestOrMinRatio--\caNestOrMaxRatio\ of the best single-member oracle in work units (the greedy rule itself finds no second regime to exploit). That differed from the development runs, in which the two-member Jacobi set was $8$--$15\%$ faster than damped Jacobi alone on convection--diffusion and anisotropic diffusion (\Cref{tab:ca_heldout}), and the difference is plausibly the decision granularity. With the numpy sweeps a Jacobi macro-action was about ten sweeps, and the oracle alternated undamped Jacobi---the cheapest member on the band-edge modes $|k| \approx 32$, which it contracts by about $0.5$ per sweep at $128^2$ but which leaves the Nyquist modes untouched---with damped Jacobi, which removes them. With the compiled sweeps a damped-Jacobi macro-action is \caMJacobiDamped\ sweeps: it contracts the band-edge modes by $0.665^{\caMJacobiDamped} \approx \caJacDampMacro$ and the Nyquist modes by $0.34^{\caMJacobiDamped} \approx \caJacNyqMacro$ (single-mode factors at $128^2$), which suggests that the band the corrector leaves is removed within one or two macro-actions, leaving a nonstationary schedule little to gain; the granularity ablation tests this hypothesis. \Cref{sec:wallclock_granularity} repeats these cells with a four times finer unit and tests directly whether the gain returns \textbf{[pending]}; the $256^2$ grids, where the band left to the smoothers is twice as wide and needs several macro-actions, are the other place it could, and there it does: on the Poisson equation at $256^2$ the two nested ensembles are $1.23\times$ and $1.24\times$ faster than the best single-member router at $10^{-8}$ on every instance (work units and live time), their oracles $1.26$--$1.27\times$ faster than the best single-member oracle, i.e., the greedy rule finds the nonstationary Jacobi schedule that the screening predicted; over all equations at $256^2$ the ensemble routers are significantly faster than the best single-member router in \caNestWinsB\ of \caNestNumB\ cells (ratios \caNestMinRatioB--\caNestMaxRatioB\ at $10^{-8}$, \caNestMinRatioHB--\caNestMaxRatioHB\ at $h^2$; oracles \caNestOrMinRatioB--\caNestOrMaxRatioB). \emph{Saturation}: in the first run, adding GS to the Jacobi pair changed the oracle's schedule by at most a few percent, because GS never won a cost-aware comparison against the Jacobi pair. \emph{Monotonicity}: the ensemble routers' ratios against the best single-member router in work units are \caNestMinRatioH--\caNestMaxRatioH\ at $h^2$ and \caNestMinRatio--\caNestMaxRatio\ at $10^{-8}$, with \caNestLosses\ of the \caNestNum\ cells more than $5\%$ slower (\Cref{tab:ca_ens_nest} lists them; the router's imitation of its oracle degrades among near-tied members while the oracles themselves stay within a few percent of the best single oracle). A greedy rule is not monotone in its action set in general, and its learned imitation is less so; the table reports how far the losses go.

\subsection{Overheads and amortisation} \label{sec:wallclock_overheads}

\Cref{tab:ca_overheads} lists the measured cost of every operation as a function of $N$, including one decision of the LSTM router of \Cref{sec:experiments} (full-state input of size $4N^2$, hidden size 256, 4 layers): at $128^2$ one LSTM decision costs \caLstmMs\,ms, about \caLstmOverJacobi\ Jacobi sweeps, which is why the wall-clock study uses the scalar-feature router ($\approx 5\,\mu$s, independent of $N$). In situ, inside the timed replays, the router's decisions cost \caDecInSituMin--\caDecInSituMax\,$\mu$s each (the first decision of a solve and every decision after a macro-action find cold caches; the $5\,\mu$s figure is a warm-loop median), i.e. \caDecFracMin--\caDecFracMax\% of the router's time to $h^2$ (\caNDecMin--\caNDecMax\ decisions) and \caDecFracDeepMin--\caDecFracDeepMax\% of its time to $10^{-8}$, as instrumented directly inside the replays. Separately, the paired difference between the router's and the cost-aware oracle's time at $h^2$ is \caRouterOracleGapMin--\caRouterOracleGapMax\,$\mu$s per solve; the two run as separate replays with decisions that agree on \caAgreeOracleMin--\caAgreeOracleMax\% of the instances, so this gap is consistent with, but not a measurement of, the decision cost (an earlier version of this appendix put the decisions at ``well under $1\%$'' on the basis of the warm-loop figure). The corrector calls account for an estimated \caNoFracMin--\caNoFracMax\% of the router's time to $h^2$ (number of calls times the calibrated per-call cost; per-cell medians over the $128^2$ pairwise cells). Two further accounting checks: the charged time of a router solve is \caChargedFracMin--\caChargedFracMax\% of the outer elapsed time of its replay, the remainder being the Python driver's loop and timer overhead, which every method pays per iteration; and the router's live time to $h^2$ is \caLiveWuMin--\caLiveWuMax\ times its work-unit time, the per-operation costs being measured in the same form as the replay charges them. \Cref{tab:ca_amort} accounts for training: the corrector (shared with HINTS) is fit in minutes, the router in seconds to a few minutes per pairing, and the break-even number of solves after which the router's own training cost is recovered relative to HINTS ($\tau{=}15$) with the same corrector is \caBreakEvenMin--\caBreakEvenMax\ solves for the GS pairing at each equation and grid (\Cref{tab:ca_amort}; \caBreakEvenNone\ of those cells have no positive saving, and \caBreakEvenNoTrain\ have a positive saving but no recorded router-training time).

\subsection{Development versus confirmatory runs} \label{sec:wallclock_heldout}

Several choices of this study were made after looking at test results: the corrector band and the anisotropic sensor grid, the router of the convection--diffusion Jacobi pairing at $512^2$ (retrained with more rollouts after the first router missed $h^2$ on $4$ of $16$ development instances, \Cref{sec:wallclock_protocol}), and the imitation budget of the ensemble routers (raised after the pairwise recipe imitated its oracle imperfectly on one development cell, \Cref{sec:wallclock_ens}); the optimistic best-schedule baseline is tuned on the test set by design and labelled as such. All of these were made on the development set (seed $72$), with the earlier numpy/scipy sweeps, the earlier forcing sampler and $\tau = 25$ as the HINTS reference (\Cref{sec:wallclock_protocol}), which is why the table compares against $\tau = 25$ in both runs. Every result in this appendix comes from a single evaluation of the frozen configurations on the confirmatory set (seed $73$) with the compiled kernels and three timed replays. \Cref{tab:ca_heldout} lists, for every cell present in both, the development and the confirmatory speedups: the two differ both through the instances and through the kernels---the compiled sweeps are $4$--$5\times$ faster, so the corrector is worth $2$--$3\times$ more sweeps than in the development runs and the margins over fixed schedules at $h^2$ shrink accordingly---and the table shows exactly how much of the development-phase margin survives.

\subsection{Verification of the theoretical assumptions} \label{sec:wallclock_assumptions}

\Cref{th:suboptgreedy} and Propositions~\ref{th:weaklyalphasupermodular}--\ref{th:simultaneoussupermodular} assume that every error propagation map $G_j = I - C_j\circ\mathcal{L}_h^a$ is Lipschitz with constant $\rho_j \le 1$ (with at least one strict contraction in the optimal sequence, respectively a shared unitary eigenbasis), zero-preserving, and---for postfix monotonicity---simultaneously diagonalisable by a unitary matrix; \Cref{th:consistency} assumes that at every state at least one solver leaves a positive fraction of the error. \Cref{tab:ca_assump} checks these conditions numerically for every operation of the study---finite diagnostics (a power-iteration estimate of the Lipschitz constant, commutators on random vectors, exhaustive search over short horizons), none of which is a certificate over the whole input space--- on the mean-free subspace (the constant mode is the null space of the periodic operator and is excluded from the data and from every iteration): the Euclidean Lipschitz constant $\|G_j\|_2$ (power iteration on $G_j^{\top}G_j$; exact from the Fourier symbol for Jacobi), the Lipschitz constant $\|G_j\|_A = \|A_s^{1/2} G_j A_s^{-1/2}\|_2$ in the energy norm of the symmetric part $A_s$ of the discrete operator, the same for the macro-action $G_j^{m_j}$, the spectral radius, the smallest observed contraction $\sigma_{\min} = \min\|G_j x\|/\|x\|$, $\|C_j(0)\|$, and the commutator $\|G_j G_{\mathrm{NO}} - G_{\mathrm{NO}} G_j\|$ on random vectors. \Cref{tab:ca_assump_paths} evaluates the quantities of \Cref{th:suboptgreedy} and \Cref{th:consistency} along the cost-aware oracle's own path to $\varepsilon = 10^{-8}$ (a horizon of tens of macro-actions; to $h^2$ the path has one or two steps).

\paragraph{What holds, and in which norm.} (i) Every classical solver is zero-preserving exactly and, on the mean-free Nyquist-free subspace on which the forcing lives (undamped Jacobi has eigenvalue $-1$ on the checkerboard mode, which the forcing excludes and the Jacobi-type maps never generate; the table's Jacobi values include the Nyquist modes as its caption states), contracts in the sense that matters for convergence: the spectral radius of $G_j$ is below $1$ in every setting (at most \caRhoSpecMax), and so is the energy-norm Lipschitz constant of the solver and of its macro-action (at most \caRhoAMax). The \emph{Euclidean} Lipschitz constant, however, exceeds $1$ for Gauss--Seidel, SOR and symmetric GS (up to \caRhoTwoGsMax\ for SOR), whose iteration matrices are non-normal; the proof of Proposition~\ref{th:weaklyalphasupermodular} uses only the triangle inequality and the composition rule for Lipschitz constants, so it holds verbatim with $\|\cdot\|_2$ replaced by the energy norm, in which the condition is satisfied by all classical solvers in all settings---but that statement concerns the greedy rule and objective defined with the energy norm, whereas the oracle and the router of this study minimise the Euclidean error. For the evaluated Euclidean rule, the strict-contraction premise of Proposition~\ref{th:weaklyalphasupermodular} therefore holds for the Jacobi-type solvers and fails for the non-normal sweeps, whose Euclidean expansion is confined to a single sweep (their spectral radii and macro-action contraction show the iteration is convergent). For (damped) Jacobi both constants agree (the maps are Fourier-diagonal); the values are close to $1$ because the slowest modes (the smoothest ones, and the near-Nyquist mode for undamped Jacobi) are barely damped by a point smoother---which is exactly why the corrector is needed. (ii) The corrector's map is zero-preserving, contracts every band mode to $\caBandMax$ or better (on average to $10^{-4}$--$10^{-6}$) and leaves the modes outside the band untouched, so its Lipschitz constant is exactly $1$ (not $<1$): \Cref{th:weaklyalphasupermodular} in its strict form does not apply to the corrector, but \Cref{th:simultaneoussupermodular} does, and its second condition---a shared unitary eigenbasis---holds exactly for the exact band-limited inverse together with (damped) Jacobi, all of which are diagonal in the Fourier basis, and, for the learned corrector, the measured commutators are $\approx 10^{-6}$, at the corrector's single-precision accuracy (a diagnostic; replacing the learned corrector by the exact inverse did not change the oracle's decisions in the development run, \Cref{sec:wallclock_protocol}), so for the ensembles $\{\mathrm{NO}, \text{Jacobi}\}$, $\{\mathrm{NO}, \text{Jacobi (0.67)}\}$ and $\{\mathrm{NO}, \text{Jacobi}, \text{Jacobi (0.67)}\}$ with the exact band-limited inverse the objective is supermodular and postfix monotone and \Cref{th:suboptgreedy} applies with $\alpha = \mu = 1$; for the fitted corrector we measure the fit error and the commutators but do not propagate them through a perturbation bound (a small commutator is a diagnostic, not a certificate), so no guarantee is stated for it, and the exhaustive short-horizon check below is the evidence that the fitted maps behave like the exact ones. For GS, SOR, symmetric GS and multigrid the commutators are small but nonzero ($10^{-3}$--$10^{-1}$) and no guarantee is claimed at any horizon. (iii) Invertibility, which an earlier version of the theory used for postfix monotonicity, is neither needed for the corrected result nor sufficient in general (\Cref{sec:proofweaklyalphasupermodular}); for the record, a Gauss--Seidel or symmetric-GS sweep annihilates an error concentrated at the first grid point ($\sigma_{\min} = 0$), SOR leaves $(1-\omega)$ of it ($\sigma_{\min} = 0.72$--$0.83$ in \Cref{tab:ca_assump}), undamped Jacobi annihilates the mode $(N/4, N/4)$, and the corrector annihilates the band. Postfix monotonicity ($\mu = 1$) is therefore guaranteed only for the Jacobi-type ensembles with the exact band-limited inverse, and is measured for the others. (iv) \Cref{tab:ca_theorem} checks \Cref{th:suboptgreedy} by exhaustive enumeration (in floating point, with errors clipped at a relative floor of $10^{-11}$) for short horizons on the evaluated ensembles, in the Euclidean objective the oracle optimises and for the deployed cost-aware rule: for every pairing (including line GS on anisotropic diffusion), for $\{\text{Jacobi}, \text{Jacobi (0.67)}\}$, for the two non-commuting sweeps $\{\text{GS}, \text{SOR}\}$, for $\{\text{GS}, \text{multigrid}\}$ and for all point smoothers together, the optimal sequence $O$ of $T$ macro-actions ($T = 4$, or $3$ for ensembles with more than four actions) is found by exhaustive search on $8$ test instances ($4$ for ensembles with more than four actions), and $\mu$ (over the greedy prefixes), $\alpha(O)$ (over the greedy prefixes, and over every sequence of length below $T$) and the bound itself are computed. Over all \caThmN\ instance--ensemble pairs the largest $\mu$ is \caThmMuMax, the largest $\alpha(O)$ over the greedy prefixes is \caThmAlphaGreedyMax\ and over all short prefixes \caThmAlphaAllMax; the numerical bound holds on \caThmHolds\ pairs, and the on-path premises that the recurrence proof of \Cref{th:suboptgreedy} uses---prefix monotonicity and the weak-supermodularity inequality at the reported $\alpha$ on the greedy prefixes (not the global definition), the deployed rule equal to \Cref{alg:greedy}, and an exhaustive optimum resolved above the round-off floor---are verified, as a finite numerical check, on \caThmPremises\ pairs (on \caThmFloor\ the optimum is at the floor and the instance is numerically unresolved rather than certified; the deployed rule differs from \Cref{alg:greedy} on \caThmPlainDiff, and the clipping would have changed the deployed path on \caThmClip); \caThmExpand\ greedy prefixes and \caThmExpandAll\ prefixes overall show an expansion of the error by a single action of $O$, i.e. a failure of prefix monotonicity in the Euclidean norm, and \caThmViol\ greedy prefixes (\caThmViolAll\ prefixes overall) violate the inequality at the reported $\alpha$ (the largest candidate $\alpha$ over greedy prefixes, \caThmAlphaGreedyMax, includes the pairs that fail). The greedy sequence's error is within \caThmMaxRatio$\times$ of the exhaustive optimum on every one of the \caThmResolved\ pairs with a resolved optimum (on the others the ratio is one of clipped objectives; the table gives medians and the worst cases per ensemble). The check supports the optimality of the greedy rule over a few macro-actions; the horizons at which the oracle runs to $10^{-8}$ are $10$--$400$ macro-actions (\Cref{tab:ca_assump_paths}), where no constant is established for the non-normal sweeps: Proposition~\ref{th:weaklyalphasupermodular} would need contraction in the Euclidean norm, which they lack (\Cref{tab:ca_assump}), and the worst-case constant in \Cref{tab:ca_assump_paths} is computed with energy-norm constants for orientation only. The worst-case $\alpha(O)$ of \Cref{th:weaklyalphasupermodular}, which only uses the Lipschitz constants, is loose in comparison: along the oracle's path to $10^{-8}$ (\Cref{tab:ca_assump_paths}) $\sum_i \rho_{O_i}^2$ is close to $T$ because each $\rho$ is dominated by the slowest mode, so the bound ranges from $\caAlphaBoundMin$ (the multigrid pairing, whose cycle contracts everything) to $10^2$--$10^4$ for the point smoothers, and is infinite on the few instances where $\sum_i \rho_{O_i}^2 \ge T$. (The last two columns of \Cref{tab:ca_assump_paths} evaluate the ratio of \Cref{eqn:alpha_supermod} with the oracle's own suffix in place of the unknown long-horizon $O$; this is only a diagnostic, and its maximum is attained trivially at the last prefix.) (v) \Cref{th:consistency} is stated for the per-state normalised weights $\tilde c_j/\sum_k \tilde c_k$ that the router is trained with; its one hypothesis is that at every visited state at least one solver leaves a positive fraction of the current error, i.e. $\max_j \tilde c_j / \|e^{(t)}\|^2 > 0$ (last column of \Cref{tab:ca_assump_paths}; the column before it shows that the per-step errors never exceed the current error), so the surrogate's Bayes consistency applies at every visited state.
